articleHeadline: SFTS Virus in China: Spring marks increased risk for tick-borne infections
articleSummary: In Xi'an, China, the Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) virus, caused by Dabie Bandavirus, has entered its active spring period as temperatures rise. Since April 1, 2026, SFTS is classified as a Category B infectious disease in China. The incubation period is 1–2 weeks post-tick bite, with early symptoms including fever (≥38°C), thrombocytopenia, fatigue, headache, myalgia, nausea, diarrhea, and lymphadenopathy. Without prompt treatment, severe cases can lead to skin bruising, bleeding, altered consciousness, and multi-organ failure, significantly increasing the risk of death. Currently, there is no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine available, making prevention crucial. Transmission primarily occurs through tick bites, but risks also arise from direct contact with infected blood or secretions, as well as contact with virus-carrying livestock or pets. High-risk groups include farmers, outdoor workers, campers, and pet owners, with outbreaks typically peaking from March to July and potential autumn rebounds in certain regions.
